questions.s: Which of the following is a qualitative variable?
o: Height of a student in cm
Number of rooms in a house
questions.e: A qualitative variable (attribute) records a category, and blood groups A, B, AB and O are categories, not amounts. Height, number of rooms and a bill are all measured or counted, so they are quantitative.

questions.s: The number of children in a family is an example of:
questions.e: Children are counted in whole numbers (0, 1, 2, …) with no values in between, so the variable is discrete. It would be continuous only if it could take any value in an interval, as height or weight can.

questions.s: A table shows wheat production separately for Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. This data is classified:
questions.e: Classification by place or region is geographical (spatial). Chronological classification arranges data by time, such as year by year, which is not the basis here.

questions.s: A frequency table uses the classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39. What are the class boundaries of the first class?
questions.e: The gap between 19 and 20 is 1, so half of it (0.5) is subtracted from each lower limit and added to each upper limit: 9.5 and 19.5. 10 and 19 are the class limits, not the boundaries.

questions.s: What is the midpoint of the class 20–29?
questions.e: Midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2 = (20 + 29) ÷ 2 = 24.5. 25 would be the midpoint only if the class were 20–30.

questions.s: For the classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, what is the class width (class interval)?
questions.e: Class width is the difference between successive lower limits (20 − 10) or between the boundaries of a class (19.5 − 9.5), which is 10. 9 comes from subtracting the limits of one class, 19 − 10, a common slip.

questions.s: Using Sturges' rule, k = 1 + 3.3 log n, about how many classes should be made for 100 observations?
questions.e: log 100 = 2, so k = 1 + 3.3 × 2 = 7.6, which rounds up to 8 classes. 10 is √100, a different rough rule, not Sturges' rule.

questions.s: In a histogram, the area of each rectangle is proportional to:
questions.e: A histogram shows frequency by area: width is the class interval and height is chosen so that the area matches the frequency. Cumulative frequencies are plotted in an ogive, not a histogram.

questions.s: An ogive is a graph of:
questions.e: An ogive (cumulative frequency polygon) plots cumulative frequencies against class boundaries. Frequency densities give the heights of histogram bars, not an ogive.

questions.s: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining with straight lines the:
o: midpoints of the tops of the bars
questions.e: Each class frequency is plotted at the class midpoint, which is the middle of the top of its histogram bar, and the points are joined. Plotting cumulative totals at upper boundaries would give an ogive instead.

questions.s: Sana's family spends Rs 10,000 of its Rs 40,000 monthly income on rent. In a pie chart of the budget, what is the angle of the rent sector?
questions.e: Rent is 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = ¼ of income, and ¼ of 360° = 90°. 25° confuses the 25 % share with degrees.

questions.s: A pie chart shows the subjects chosen by 1,800 students. The sector for Computer Science has an angle of 72°. How many students chose Computer Science?
questions.e: Number = (72 ÷ 360) × 1,800 = ⅕ × 1,800 = 360. Reading the angle 72 as the number of students ignores that the whole circle stands for 1,800.

questions.s: What is the arithmetic mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 12?
questions.e: Mean = (4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 12) ÷ 5 = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. 6 is the middle value as listed, but the values must be added, not read off.

questions.s: The mean of 20 numbers was found to be 15. Later it was noticed that 34 had been copied as 43. What is the correct mean?
questions.e: Wrong total = 20 × 15 = 300. Correct total = 300 − 43 + 34 = 291, so the mean is 291 ÷ 20 = 14.55. 15.45 adds the error of 9 instead of removing it.

questions.s: The mean of five numbers is 18. When a sixth number is added, the mean becomes 20. What is the sixth number?
questions.e: Total of five = 5 × 18 = 90; total of six = 6 × 20 = 120. The sixth number is 120 − 90 = 30. 2 is just the rise in the mean, not the new value.

questions.s: For any set of data, the sum of the deviations of the values from their arithmetic mean, Σ(x − x̄), is always:
questions.e: Σ(x − x̄) = Σx − n·x̄ = Σx − Σx = 0, so positive and negative deviations always cancel. This is why mean deviation uses absolute values.

questions.s: The mean of a set of values is 12. Each value is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added. What is the new mean?
questions.e: The mean follows the same change as the values: 3 × 12 + 5 = 41. 36 forgets to add 5, and 51 adds 5 before multiplying.

questions.s: The table shows the number of mobile phones owned by the households in a street. What is the mean number of phones per household?
questions.e: Σf = 20 and Σfx = 3 + 10 + 24 + 16 = 53, so the mean is 53 ÷ 20 = 2.65. 13.25 divides by the 4 rows instead of the 20 households, and 2.5 is simply the mean of 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.s: Section A of a class has 30 students with mean marks 60, and Section B has 20 students with mean marks 70. What is the combined mean of all 50 students?
questions.e: Combined mean = (30 × 60 + 20 × 70) ÷ 50 = (1,800 + 1,400) ÷ 50 = 64. 65 is the simple average of 60 and 70, which ignores that Section A is larger.

questions.s: Bilal scored 80 in a subject with weight 3 and 60 in a subject with weight 2. What is his weighted mean score?
questions.e: Weighted mean = (80 × 3 + 60 × 2) ÷ (3 + 2) = 360 ÷ 5 = 72. 70 is the unweighted mean, which treats the two subjects as equally important.

questions.s: What is the geometric mean of 4 and 9?
questions.e: GM of two numbers = √(4 × 9) = √36 = 6. 6.5 is the arithmetic mean, and 36 is the product before taking the root.

questions.s: What is the geometric mean of 2, 4 and 8?
questions.e: GM = ∛(2 × 4 × 8) = ∛64 = 4. 4.67 is the arithmetic mean (14 ÷ 3), and 64 is the product without the cube root.

questions.s: What is the harmonic mean of 2 and 6?
questions.e: HM = 2 ÷ (½ + ⅙) = 2 ÷ ⅔ = 3, or 2ab ÷ (a + b) = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. 4 is the arithmetic mean and 3.46 is the geometric mean (√12).

questions.s: For two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is 10 and the geometric mean is 8. What is their harmonic mean?
questions.e: For two positive numbers GM² = AM × HM, so HM = 64 ÷ 10 = 6.4. 12.5 is 100 ÷ 8, which uses AM² instead of GM². The numbers are 16 and 4.

questions.s: For a set of positive values that are not all equal, which relation between the three means always holds?
questions.e: For unequal positive values the arithmetic mean is the largest and the harmonic mean the smallest, with the geometric mean between them; they are equal only when all values are equal. For 2 and 8: A.M. 5, G.M. 4, H.M. 3.2.

questions.s: A car goes from Lahore to Faisalabad at 60 km/h and returns along the same road at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the round trip?
questions.e: For equal distances the average speed is the harmonic mean: 2 ÷ (1/60 + 1/40) = 2 ÷ (5/120) = 48 km/h. 50 km/h is the arithmetic mean, which wrongly gives equal weight to each speed though the slower leg takes longer.

questions.s: What is the median of 7, 3, 9, 5 and 11?
questions.e: Arranged in order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The middle (3rd) value is 7. 9 is the middle value of the list as written, before sorting.

questions.s: What is the median of 12, 4, 8, 10, 6 and 14?
questions.e: In order: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. With six values the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (8 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9. Choosing 8 or 10 takes only one of the two middle values.

questions.s: The table shows the number of goals scored by a hockey team in 20 matches. What is the median number of goals?
questions.e: n = 20, so the median is the mean of the 10th and 11th values. Cumulative frequencies are 2, 7, 13, …, so both lie in the row for 2 goals. 6 is the middle frequency, not a number of goals.

questions.s: The table shows the marks of 30 students. Using median = L + (h/f)(n/2 − C), what is the median mark?
questions.e: n/2 = 15 and cumulative frequencies are 5, 13, 25, 30, so the median class is 20–30 with L = 20, C = 13, f = 12, h = 10. Median = 20 + (10/12)(15 − 13) = 21.67. 25 is just the midpoint of the median class.

questions.s: What is the mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 8, 5, 7?
questions.e: 5 appears three times, more often than any other value, so the mode is 5. 5.71 is the mean (40 ÷ 7), and 7 appears only twice.

questions.s: A data set in which two different values occur with the same highest frequency is called:
questions.e: Two modes make a distribution bimodal; one mode makes it unimodal. Symmetry and skewness describe the shape of the distribution, not the number of modes.

questions.s: Weights of parcels are grouped as 10–20 kg (frequency 4), 20–30 kg (frequency 10) and 30–40 kg (frequency 6). Using mode = L + (f₁ − f₀)h ÷ [(f₁ − f₀) + (f₁ − f₂)], what is the mode?
questions.e: The modal class is 20–30 with L = 20, f₁ = 10, f₀ = 4, f₂ = 6, h = 10. Mode = 20 + 6 × 10 ÷ (6 + 4) = 26 kg. 25 kg is the midpoint of the modal class, which ignores the pull of the neighbouring frequencies.

questions.s: In a moderately skewed distribution the mean is 30 and the median is 28. Using the empirical relation, what is the mode?
questions.e: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean = 84 − 60 = 24. 34 comes from swapping the mean and the median in the formula (90 − 56).

questions.s: Which average is the only suitable one for the favourite colours of a group of students?
questions.e: Colours are nominal categories with no order and no numerical value, so only the most frequent category, the mode, makes sense. The median needs data that can be put in order, and the means need numbers.

questions.s: Which average is most affected by a few extremely large or small values?
questions.e: The mean uses the size of every value, so one very large salary can pull it up sharply. The median and quartiles depend only on position, and the mode only on frequency.

questions.s: In a perfectly symmetrical unimodal distribution:
questions.e: With no skew, the three averages coincide at the centre of the distribution. Unequal averages are a sign of skewness.

questions.s: In a positively skewed distribution, the usual order of the averages is:
questions.e: A long tail on the right drags the mean upwards most, the median less, and the mode stays at the peak, giving mean > median > mode. The reverse order belongs to negative skewness.

questions.s: In a frequency table of 40 observations, a class has frequency 8. What is its relative frequency?
questions.e: Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total = 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2. 5 is the inverse, 40 ÷ 8.

questions.s: The 'less than' cumulative frequencies of four consecutive classes are 4, 10, 22 and 30. What is the frequency of the third class?
questions.e: Each class frequency is the difference between successive cumulative frequencies: 22 − 10 = 12. 22 is the cumulative frequency itself, and 8 is the frequency of the fourth class (30 − 22).

questions.s: When the classes of a histogram have unequal widths, the height of each bar should be:
questions.e: Heights must be frequency densities so that area still matches frequency. Using raw frequencies makes wide classes look far larger than they are.

questions.s: What is the mean of the first 10 natural numbers?
questions.e: Sum = 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55, and 55 ÷ 10 = 5.5. 55 is the sum before dividing.

questions.s: The mean of 10 observations is 25. If the observations 30 and 40 are removed, what is the mean of the remaining ones?
questions.e: Total = 10 × 25 = 250; after removal, 250 − 70 = 180 for 8 observations, giving 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5. 18 divides 180 by 10, forgetting that only 8 observations remain.

questions.s: The mean mark of 40 boys is 50. The combined mean of these 40 boys and 60 girls is 56. What is the mean mark of the girls?
questions.e: Total for all 100 = 5,600 and for boys = 2,000, so girls total 3,600 and their mean is 3,600 ÷ 60 = 60. 62 assumes the combined mean lies halfway between the two group means, which ignores the group sizes.

questions.s: Monthly rainfall in Murree recorded for January to December, arranged month by month, is an example of:
questions.e: Arranging data in order of time is chronological (temporal) classification. Geographical classification would compare places, such as Murree, Quetta and Karachi.

questions.s: Which of the following variables is continuous?
o: Number of cars in a car park
questions.e: Time can take any value in an interval, such as 13.2 s or 13.27 s, so it is continuous. The other three are counts in whole numbers, which makes them discrete.

questions.s: Positions in a class (1st, 2nd, 3rd, …) are measured on which scale?
questions.e: Positions have a meaningful order but the gaps between them are not equal, which is an ordinal scale. Nominal data has no order at all, while interval and ratio scales need equal units.

questions.s: For 10 observations, Σ(x − 20) = 30. What is the mean of the observations?
questions.e: Σ(x − 20) = Σx − 200 = 30, so Σx = 230 and x̄ = 23. Equivalently, x̄ = 20 + 30/10. 3 is only the mean deviation from 20, and 17 subtracts it instead of adding.

questions.s: The table shows the daily wages of 20 workers in hundreds of rupees. What is the mean wage, in hundreds of rupees?
questions.e: Using midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35: Σfx = 15 + 105 + 150 + 140 = 410 and Σf = 20, so the mean is 410 ÷ 20 = 20.5. 20 is the middle of the range 0–40, which ignores the frequencies.

questions.s: The common logarithms of three positive numbers add up to 3. What is their geometric mean?
questions.e: log G.M. = (Σ log x) ÷ n = 3 ÷ 3 = 1, so G.M. = antilog 1 = 10. 1,000 is the antilog of the total, which is the product of the numbers, not their mean.

questions.s: For grouped data, the mode lies in:
o: the class with the highest frequency
the first class of the table
the class of highest cumulative total
questions.e: The mode is the most frequent value, so it lies in the modal class, the one with the largest frequency. The last class always has the highest cumulative total, which says nothing about the mode.

questions.s: For the data 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, which statement is true?
questions.e: Mean = 20 ÷ 5 = 4, median = 3 and mode = 3. The large value 8 pulls the mean above the median and mode, a sign of positive skew.

questions.s: Marital status of the employees of a bank is:
questions.e: Single, married, widowed and divorced are categories, so marital status is qualitative. Discrete and continuous describe numerical variables.

questions.s: What is the mean of 15, 25 and 35?
questions.e: Mean = 75 ÷ 3 = 25. 75 is the total before dividing by 3.

questions.s: What is the median of 2, 9, 4, 7, 5, 8, 3 and 6?
questions.e: In order: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The two middle values are 5 and 6, so the median is 5.5. 7 is the middle of the unsorted list.

questions.s: The mean of six numbers is 12. Five of them add up to 55. What is the sixth number?
questions.e: Total of six = 6 × 12 = 72, so the sixth number is 72 − 55 = 17. 11 is 55 ÷ 5, the mean of the five, not the missing value.

questions.s: Ayesha buys 2 kg of dates at Rs 300 per kg and 3 kg at Rs 400 per kg. What is the average price per kg she paid?
questions.e: Weighted mean = (2 × 300 + 3 × 400) ÷ 5 = 1,800 ÷ 5 = Rs 360 per kg. Rs 350 is the plain average of the two prices, which ignores that she bought more of the dearer dates.

questions.s: What is the geometric mean of 3 and 27?
questions.e: G.M. = √(3 × 27) = √81 = 9. 15 is the arithmetic mean and 81 is the product before the square root.

questions.s: The table shows the ages of 20 cricket club members. Using median = L + (h/f)(n/2 − C), what is the median age?
questions.e: n/2 = 10, and the cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 20, so the median class is 20–30 with C = 6 and f = 10. Median = 20 + (10/10)(10 − 6) = 24 years. 25 years is only the class midpoint.

questions.s: In a moderately skewed distribution the median is 40 and the mode is 46. Using mode = 3 median − 2 mean, what is the mean?
questions.e: 46 = 120 − 2 × mean gives 2 × mean = 74, so the mean is 37. 43 comes from adding 46 to 120 by mistake.

questions.s: What are the class boundaries of the class 50–59 in a table with classes 40–49, 50–59, 60–69?
questions.e: Half the gap of 1 between classes is 0.5, so the boundaries are 50 − 0.5 = 49.5 and 59 + 0.5 = 59.5. 50 and 59 are the class limits.

questions.s: In a pie chart, a sector represents 30 % of the total. What is its angle?
questions.e: Angle = 30 % of 360° = 0.3 × 360° = 108°. 30° confuses the percentage with degrees.

questions.s: Three groups of 10, 20 and 30 workers have mean daily wages of Rs 400, Rs 500 and Rs 600. What is the mean wage of all 60 workers?
questions.e: Total = 4,000 + 10,000 + 18,000 = Rs 32,000, and 32,000 ÷ 60 = Rs 533.33. Rs 500 is the plain average of the three group means, which ignores the larger third group.

questions.s: Which graph is used to find the median and quartiles graphically?
questions.e: On an ogive, the value read off at the cumulative frequency n/2 is the median, and n/4 and 3n/4 give the quartiles. Pie and bar charts show shares and comparisons, not cumulative totals.

questions.s: Data collected by an investigator himself, for the first time and for a specific purpose, are called:
questions.e: Data gathered first-hand for the inquiry at hand are primary. Secondary data were collected earlier by someone else, for example figures taken from a Pakistan Bureau of Statistics report.

questions.s: The geometric mean is the most suitable average for:
questions.e: Growth rates multiply over time, so the geometric mean gives the right average rate. It cannot be used when a value is zero, and speeds over equal distances call for the harmonic mean.

questions.s: The median of a data set is 15. If every value is doubled, what is the new median?
questions.e: Doubling every value keeps the order, so the middle value also doubles to 30. 17 adds 2 instead of multiplying, and 225 squares the median.

questions.s: What is the range of 12, 7, 19, 4 and 15?
questions.e: Range = largest − smallest = 19 − 4 = 15. 12 is the difference between the first and last values as listed, not between the extremes.

questions.s: The highest temperature in a week was 40 °C and the lowest was 10 °C. What is the coefficient of range?
questions.e: Coefficient of range = (max − min) ÷ (max + min) = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6. 30 is the range itself, an absolute measure, and 0.75 divides by the maximum only.

questions.s: For the data 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, taking Q₁ and Q₃ at positions (n + 1)/4 and 3(n + 1)/4, what is the quartile deviation?
questions.e: n = 7, so Q₁ is the 2nd value (5) and Q₃ the 6th value (12). Q.D. = (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2 = 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5. 7 is the interquartile range, before halving.

questions.s: The quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) is defined as:
questions.e: Quartile deviation is half the interquartile range, (Q₃ − Q₁)/2. Q₃ − Q₁ is the interquartile range itself, and (Q₃ − Q₁)/(Q₃ + Q₁) is the coefficient of quartile deviation.

questions.s: For a distribution, Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 30. What is the coefficient of quartile deviation?
questions.e: Coefficient of Q.D. = (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ (Q₃ + Q₁) = 10 ÷ 50 = 0.2. 5 is the quartile deviation itself, (30 − 20) ÷ 2.

questions.s: What is the mean deviation from the mean of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10?
questions.e: Mean = 6; absolute deviations are 4, 2, 0, 2, 4, totalling 12, so M.D. = 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4. 0 comes from forgetting the absolute values, and 2.83 is the standard deviation (√8).

questions.s: The variance of a data set is the square of its:
questions.e: Variance = σ² and standard deviation σ = √variance. Mean deviation uses absolute values, not squares, so it is not linked to variance in this way.

questions.s: What is the standard deviation of 3, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 8, 10, taking the divisor as n?
questions.e: Mean = 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, totalling 32, so variance = 32 ÷ 8 = 4 and S.D. = 2. 4 is the variance, before the square root.

questions.s: Taking the divisor as n, what is the variance of 4, 6 and 8?
questions.e: Mean = 6; squared deviations 4, 0, 4 add to 8, so variance = 8 ÷ 3. 4 divides by n − 1 = 2, the sample formula that the stem rules out, and 8 forgets to divide.

questions.s: The variance of x is 9. What is the variance of y = 2x + 5?
questions.e: Adding 5 does not change spread, but multiplying by 2 multiplies variance by 2² = 4, giving 36. 18 multiplies by 2 instead of 4, and 41 also wrongly adds the 5.

questions.s: The standard deviation of x is 4. What is the standard deviation of y = 3 − 2x?
questions.e: S.D. is multiplied by the absolute value of the coefficient: |−2| × 4 = 8, and the constant 3 has no effect. A standard deviation is never negative, so −8 is impossible; 16 is the variance-style factor 2² × 4.

questions.s: If 10 is added to every value in a data set, the standard deviation:
questions.e: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by the same amount, so every deviation from the mean is unchanged. Only the mean, median and mode rise by 10.

questions.s: Over a season, Ali's mean score was 40 runs with S.D. 8, and Usman's was 50 runs with S.D. 12. Who was the more consistent batsman?
o: Usman, as his mean is higher
questions.e: Consistency is judged by the coefficient of variation: Ali 8/40 = 20 %, Usman 12/50 = 24 %. The lower C.V. means less relative variation, so Ali was more consistent; a higher mean shows better scoring, not steadier scoring.

questions.s: For 5 values, Σx = 20 and Σx² = 100. Taking the divisor as n, what is the variance?
questions.e: Variance = Σx²/n − (Σx/n)² = 20 − 4² = 4. 20 forgets to subtract the square of the mean, and 2 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: For 10 values, Σx = 50 and Σx² = 410. Taking the divisor as n, what is the standard deviation?
questions.e: Variance = 410/10 − 5² = 41 − 25 = 16, so S.D. = √16 = 4. 16 stops at the variance, and 6.4 is √41, which leaves out the mean term.

questions.s: In a normal distribution the standard deviation is 15. About what is the quartile deviation?
questions.e: For a normal distribution Q.D. ≈ ⅔ σ = 10 and M.D. ≈ ⅘ σ = 12. Choosing 12 mixes up the quartile deviation with the mean deviation.

questions.s: The variance of a data set can never be:
questions.e: Variance is an average of squared deviations, and squares cannot be negative. It is zero when all values are equal, and it can easily be larger than the mean or a fraction.

questions.s: What is the standard deviation of 7, 7, 7, 7?
questions.e: All values equal the mean, so every deviation is 0 and the S.D. is 0. 7 is the mean, not a measure of spread.

questions.s: A distribution has mean 52, mode 46 and standard deviation 12. What is Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness, (mean − mode)/S.D.?
questions.e: Sk = (52 − 46) ÷ 12 = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5, a positive skew. −0.5 subtracts the mean from the mode, and 6 forgets to divide by the S.D.

questions.s: A distribution has mean 30, median 27 and standard deviation 6. What is Pearson's coefficient of skewness, 3(mean − median)/S.D.?
questions.e: Sk = 3(30 − 27) ÷ 6 = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. 0.5 leaves out the factor 3 that comes from the empirical relation between mean, median and mode.

questions.s: For a distribution, Q₁ = 20, Q₂ = 25 and Q₃ = 34. What is Bowley's coefficient of skewness, (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Q₂)/(Q₃ − Q₁)?
questions.e: Sk = (34 + 20 − 50) ÷ (34 − 20) = 4 ÷ 14 = 2/7, a mild positive skew, as Q₃ is further from the median than Q₁ is. 4/9 divides by Q₃ − Q₂ instead of Q₃ − Q₁.

questions.s: If a distribution has a negative coefficient of skewness, then:
o: the mean is below the median
the long tail is on the right
questions.e: In a negatively skewed distribution the long tail is on the left, which pulls the mean below the median and mode. A long right tail goes with positive skewness.

questions.s: A distribution that is more sharply peaked than the normal curve is called:
questions.e: Lepto- means slender: a leptokurtic curve is tall and narrow. Platykurtic curves are flatter than normal, and the normal curve itself is mesokurtic.

questions.s: The second moment about the mean is equal to the:
questions.e: m₂ = Σ(x − x̄)²/n, which is exactly the variance. The first moment about the mean is always 0, and the standard deviation is √m₂.

questions.s: For a normal distribution, the moment ratio b₂ = m₄/m₂² is equal to:
questions.e: The normal curve is the mesokurtic standard, with b₂ = 3. Values above 3 mean a leptokurtic curve and values below 3 a platykurtic one. 0 is the normal curve's value of b₁, the skewness ratio.

questions.s: About an arbitrary origin, the first two moments of a distribution are m₁′ = 2 and m₂′ = 13. What is the variance?
questions.e: Variance = m₂ = m₂′ − (m₁′)² = 13 − 4 = 9. 11 subtracts m₁′ instead of its square, and 3 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: In an index number series, the index for the base year is always:
questions.e: Every index compares a period with the base period, which is set to 100. An index of 120 then means a 20 % rise over the base.

questions.s: The price of a kilogram of sugar was Rs 80 in the base year and Rs 120 in the current year. What is the price relative?
questions.e: Price relative = (p₁ ÷ p₀) × 100 = (120 ÷ 80) × 100 = 150. 66.67 divides the old price by the new one, and 50 is only the percentage rise.

questions.s: A price index of 125 for the current year means that, compared with the base year, prices have:
questions.e: The base is 100, so 125 is 25 points, or 25 %, above it. Rising by 125 % would give an index of 225, and an index shows relative change, not rupees.

questions.s: Laspeyres' price index uses as weights the:
questions.e: Laspeyres: Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100, weighted by base-year quantities q₀. Current-year quantities are the weights in Paasche's index, and the average of both years belongs to Marshall–Edgeworth.

questions.s: Fisher's ideal index number is the:
o: arithmetic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche
harmonic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche
geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche
questions.e: Fisher's index = √(L × P), the geometric mean of the two. It is called ideal partly because it satisfies the time-reversal and factor-reversal tests, which the arithmetic mean of L and P does not.

questions.s: For a set of goods, Laspeyres' price index is 121 and Paasche's price index is 100. What is Fisher's ideal index?
questions.e: Fisher = √(121 × 100) = √12,100 = 110. 110.5 is the arithmetic mean of 121 and 100, not the geometric mean.

questions.s: Using the table, what is Laspeyres' price index for the current year?
questions.e: Σp₁q₀ = 600 + 420 = 1,020 and Σp₀q₀ = 500 + 400 = 900, so the index is 1,020 ÷ 900 × 100 = 113.33. 112.5 is the unweighted mean of the price relatives 120 and 105, and 88.24 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: The formula Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 gives which price index?
questions.e: Weighting by current-year quantities q₁ gives Paasche's index. Laspeyres uses q₀, Fisher's index is √(L × P), and a simple aggregative index uses no quantities at all.

questions.s: In the chain base method, the price of each year is compared with the price of:
questions.e: Chain base indices use link relatives, (pₙ ÷ pₙ₋₁) × 100, so each year is compared with the year before it. Comparing every year with one fixed year is the fixed base method.

questions.s: With 2020 as base (100), the link relatives are 110 for 2021 and 120 for 2022. What is the chain index for 2022?
questions.e: Chain index 2022 = (chain index 2021 × link relative 2022) ÷ 100 = 110 × 120 ÷ 100 = 132. 130 adds the two rises of 10 % and 20 %, but percentage changes compound.

questions.s: A consumer price index is mainly used to measure changes in:
questions.e: A CPI tracks the prices of a basket of goods and services bought by households, so it measures the cost of living. Industrial output is tracked by a quantity index, not a price index.

questions.s: A worker's monthly wage is Rs 30,000 and the consumer price index is 150, with base 100. What is his real wage at base-year prices?
questions.e: Real wage = money wage × 100 ÷ CPI = 30,000 × 100 ÷ 150 = Rs 20,000. Rs 45,000 multiplies by 1.5 instead of dividing, which would mean that rising prices make him richer.

questions.s: Which measure of dispersion depends only on the two extreme values?
questions.e: Range = largest − smallest, so only the two extremes affect it. This is why one unusual value can change it a lot. S.D. and M.D. use every value, and Q.D. uses the quartiles.

questions.s: Which of the following is an absolute measure of dispersion?
questions.e: An absolute measure is in the same units as the data, like the S.D. in kg or rupees. Coefficients are ratios with no units, used to compare groups.

questions.s: A grouped table has the classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59. Using class boundaries, what is the range?
questions.e: Range = upper boundary of the last class − lower boundary of the first = 59.5 − 9.5 = 50. 49 uses the class limits 59 − 10 instead of the boundaries.

questions.s: The table shows the times, in minutes, taken by 20 students to solve a puzzle. What is the first quartile Q₁, using L + (h/f)(n/4 − C)?
questions.e: n/4 = 5; cumulative frequencies are 4, 10, 18, 20, so Q₁ lies in 10–20 with C = 4, f = 6. Q₁ = 10 + (10/6)(5 − 4) = 11.67 min. 15 min is just the midpoint of that class.

questions.s: The seventh decile D₇ is the same as:
questions.e: Each decile covers 10 percentiles, so D₇ = P₇₀, the value below which 70 % of the data lie. Q₃ is P₇₅, which is a little higher.

questions.s: Taking the divisor as n, what is the variance of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5?
questions.e: Mean = 3; squared deviations 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 add to 10, so variance = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. 2.5 divides by n − 1, and √2 is the S.D.

questions.s: A distribution has mean 20 and coefficient of variation 15 %. What is its variance?
questions.e: S.D. = C.V. × mean ÷ 100 = 0.15 × 20 = 3, so variance = 3² = 9. 3 stops at the S.D., and 1.33 divides 20 by 15.

questions.s: For any data set, the mean deviation about the mean is:
questions.e: Squaring gives large deviations more weight, so the S.D. is always at least as large as the M.D.; for 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, M.D. = 2.4 and S.D. ≈ 2.83. The range is the largest of these measures, so the M.D. cannot exceed it.

questions.s: For a set of exam marks, Q₁ = 18 and Q₃ = 42. What is the interquartile range?
questions.e: Interquartile range = Q₃ − Q₁ = 42 − 18 = 24. 12 is half of it, the quartile deviation, and 30 is the midpoint of Q₁ and Q₃.

questions.s: The standard deviation of x is 5. What is the variance of (x − 10)/5?
questions.e: Subtracting 10 leaves the spread unchanged, and dividing by 5 divides the S.D. by 5, giving S.D. 1 and variance 1² = 1. 5 is the original S.D., and 0.2 divides by 5 twice.

questions.s: What is the range of 25, 31, 18, 40 and 22?
questions.e: Range = 40 − 18 = 22. 15 is the difference between the first and last numbers as listed.

questions.s: The largest value in a data set is 75 and the smallest is 25. What is the coefficient of range?
questions.e: Coefficient of range = (75 − 25) ÷ (75 + 25) = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5. 50 is the range itself, and 2 divides 50 by 25.

questions.s: What is the mean deviation from the mean of 1, 3, 5 and 7?
questions.e: Mean = 4; absolute deviations 3, 1, 1, 3 add to 8, and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Without absolute values the deviations sum to 0, and √5 is the S.D.

questions.s: Taking the divisor as n, what is the standard deviation of 1, 3, 5 and 7?
questions.e: Mean = 4; squared deviations 9, 1, 1, 9 add to 20, so variance = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 and S.D. = √5 ≈ 2.24. 5 is the variance and 2 is the mean deviation.

questions.s: The mean weight of a group of students is 80 kg and the standard deviation is 12 kg. What is the coefficient of variation?
questions.e: C.V. = 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15 %. 6.67 % divides the mean by the S.D. and then by 100, the wrong way round.

questions.s: The standard deviation of x is 2. What is the variance of y = 5x − 3?
questions.e: S.D. of y = |5| × 2 = 10, so variance = 10² = 100. The −3 has no effect on spread; 97 wrongly subtracts it, and 10 is the S.D., not the variance.

questions.s: A distribution has mean 45, mode 50 and standard deviation 10. What is Pearson's coefficient of skewness, (mean − mode)/S.D.?
questions.e: Sk = (45 − 50) ÷ 10 = −0.5, so the distribution is negatively skewed. 0.5 drops the sign that shows the direction of skew.

questions.s: The price of a litre of milk rose from Rs 40 in the base year to Rs 50. What is the price relative?
questions.e: Price relative = 50 ÷ 40 × 100 = 125. 80 is 40 ÷ 50 × 100, which compares the base year with the current year instead.

questions.s: Using the table, what is Paasche's price index for the current year?
questions.e: Σp₁q₁ = 60 + 50 = 110 and Σp₀q₁ = 50 + 40 = 90, so the index is 110 ÷ 90 × 100 = 122.22. 123.33 is the simple aggregative index (37 ÷ 30), which ignores the quantities.

questions.s: A distribution that is flatter than the normal curve is called:
questions.e: Platy- means flat: a platykurtic curve has b₂ less than 3. Leptokurtic curves are more peaked, and skewness is about lack of symmetry, not flatness.

questions.s: Laspeyres' price index is 144 and Paasche's price index is 121. What is Fisher's ideal index?
questions.e: Fisher = √(144 × 121) = 12 × 11 = 132. 132.5 is the arithmetic mean of the two indices, not the geometric mean.

questions.s: The standard deviation of a data set is always:
questions.e: S.D. is the square root of an average of squares, so it is never negative; it is zero only when all values are equal. It can be larger than 1 and larger than the mean.

questions.s: The mean marks of a class are 50 with a standard deviation of 10. What is the coefficient of variation?
questions.e: C.V. = (S.D. ÷ mean) × 100 = (10 ÷ 50) × 100 = 20 %. 500 % divides the mean by the S.D., the wrong way round.

questions.s: With 2018 as base, a price index was 120 in 2020 and 150 in 2022. If the base is shifted to 2020, what is the index for 2022?
questions.e: New index = (old index ÷ old index of new base) × 100 = 150 ÷ 120 × 100 = 125. 130 subtracts 20 points instead of dividing by 1.2.

questions.s: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
questions.e: The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6: three of six equally likely outcomes, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. 1/6 is the chance of one particular number.

questions.s: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.e: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT; only TT has no head, so P = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. 2/3 wrongly treats 'two heads, one head, no head' as equally likely.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 7?
questions.e: Six of the 36 equally likely pairs give 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So P = 6/36 = 1/6. 5/36 is the chance of a total of 6 or 8.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 10?
questions.e: The pairs (4,6), (5,5) and (6,4) give 10, so P = 3/36 = 1/12. 1/18 counts (4,6) and (6,4) as one outcome, but they are different outcomes for two dice.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a king?
questions.e: There are 4 kings in 52 cards, so P = 4/52 = 1/13. 1/52 is the chance of one particular king, such as the king of hearts.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a pack of 52. What is the probability that it is red or a king?
questions.e: P(red or king) = 26/52 + 4/52 − 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13, since the two red kings were counted twice. 15/26 (30/52) forgets to subtract them.

questions.s: In how many ways can a president and a secretary be chosen from 5 members of a society, if one person cannot hold both posts?
questions.e: The posts are different, so order matters: ⁵P₂ = 5 × 4 = 20. 10 is ⁵C₂, which would be right only if the two posts were identical.

questions.s: In how many ways can a committee of 2 be chosen from 6 people?
questions.e: A committee has no order, so ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5) ÷ 2 = 15. 30 is ⁶P₂, which counts each pair twice.

questions.s: How many different arrangements can be made of all the letters of the word PAKISTAN?
questions.e: There are 8 letters with A repeated twice, so the count is 8! ÷ 2! = 40,320 ÷ 2 = 20,160. 40,320 treats the two A's as different.

questions.s: In how many ways can 5 different books be arranged in a row on a shelf?
questions.e: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. 24 is 4!, the count for circular arrangements of 5 objects, not for a row.

questions.s: In how many ways can 6 people be seated around a round table, if only their positions relative to each other matter?
questions.e: For a circle, fix one person and arrange the rest: (6 − 1)! = 5! = 120. 720 is 6!, which counts each rotation of the same seating as different.

questions.s: In how many ways can 8 players be selected from a squad of 10?
questions.e: ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = (10 × 9) ÷ 2 = 45, since choosing 8 to play is the same as choosing 2 to leave out. 90 is ¹⁰P₂, which counts order.

questions.s: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.e: For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75. 0.615 subtracts 0.135, which would only apply if the events were independent.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.e: P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65. 0.8 simply adds the probabilities, as if the events could not happen together.

questions.s: The probability that it rains in Islamabad on a given day is 0.35. What is the probability that it does not rain that day?
questions.e: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. 1.35 adds instead of subtracting, and is impossible since no probability exceeds 1.

questions.s: For two events, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A | B)?
questions.e: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B) = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4. 0.1 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.s: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.e: P = 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15, because after one red ball is drawn only 3 red balls remain out of 9. 4/25 = (4/10)², the answer with replacement.

questions.s: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn with replacement. What is the probability of getting one red and one blue ball, in either order?
questions.e: P(red then blue) + P(blue then red) = 0.4 × 0.6 + 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. 0.24 counts only one of the two orders, and 0.52 is the chance that both balls are the same colour.

questions.s: A and B are mutually exclusive events. What is P(A ∩ B)?
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so their intersection is empty and P(A ∩ B) = 0. P(A) × P(B) is the rule for independent events, a different idea.

questions.s: Machine X makes 60 % of a factory's bulbs, of which 2 % are faulty; machine Y makes the rest, of which 5 % are faulty. What is the probability that a bulb chosen at random is faulty?
questions.e: P(faulty) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. 0.035 is the plain average of 2 % and 5 %, which ignores that machine X makes more bulbs.

questions.s: Machine X makes 60 % of a factory's bulbs, of which 2 % are faulty; machine Y makes the rest, of which 5 % are faulty. A bulb is found to be faulty. What is the probability that machine Y made it?
questions.e: By Bayes' theorem, P(Y | faulty) = 0.020 ÷ 0.032 = 0.625. 0.4 is Y's share before we learn that the bulb is faulty, and 0.375 is the chance that X made it.

questions.s: Which of the following cannot be the probability of an event?
questions.e: Every probability lies between 0 and 1 inclusive, so 1.2 is impossible. 0 is the probability of an impossible event and is allowed.

questions.s: Three coins are tossed together. How many outcomes are there in the sample space?
questions.e: Each coin has 2 outcomes, so there are 2³ = 8 outcomes, from HHH to TTT. 6 adds 2 + 2 + 2 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly two heads?
questions.e: HHT, HTH and THH are the favourable outcomes, 3 of 8, so P = 3/8. 1/4 treats 0, 1, 2 and 3 heads as equally likely, but they are not.

questions.s: A random variable X takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, k and 0.2. What is k?
questions.e: The probabilities of a distribution must add to 1, so k = 1 − (0.1 + 0.3 + 0.2) = 0.4. 0.6 is the sum of the given probabilities, not what is missing.

questions.s: A random variable X takes the values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. What is E(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = Σx·P(x) = 0.2 + 1.0 + 0.9 = 2.1. 2 is the plain mean of 1, 2, 3, which ignores the probabilities.

questions.s: A random variable X takes the values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. What is Var(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = 2.1 and E(X²) = 0.2 + 2.0 + 2.7 = 4.9, so Var(X) = 4.9 − 2.1² = 4.9 − 4.41 = 0.49. 4.9 stops at E(X²), and 0.7 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: If E(X) = 4, what is E(2X + 3)?
questions.e: Expectation is linear: E(2X + 3) = 2E(X) + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11. 8 drops the constant, and 14 adds 3 before doubling.

questions.s: If Var(X) = 4, what is Var(2X + 3)?
questions.e: Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X) = 4 × 4 = 16; the constant 3 does not affect spread. 8 multiplies by 2 instead of 2², and 11 wrongly treats variance like expectation.

questions.s: In a game, Hamza wins Rs 100 with probability 0.2 and otherwise loses Rs 20. What is his expected gain per game?
questions.e: E = 0.2 × 100 + 0.8 × (−20) = 20 − 16 = Rs 4. Rs 20 counts the winnings but not the losses, which happen 80 % of the time.

questions.s: A binomial distribution has n = 20 and p = 0.3. What is its mean?
questions.e: Mean = np = 20 × 0.3 = 6. 4.2 is the variance npq, and 14 is nq, the mean number of failures.

questions.s: A binomial distribution has n = 50 and p = 0.2. What is its variance?
questions.e: Variance = npq = 50 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 8. 10 is the mean np, and 2.83 is the standard deviation √8.

questions.s: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
questions.e: P(X = 2) = ⁴C₂ (½)⁴ = 6/16 = 3/8. 1/2 assumes that half the tosses being heads is the most likely result every time, and 1/16 forgets the ⁴C₂ = 6 orders.

questions.s: Each seed in a packet germinates with probability 0.8, independently. If 5 seeds are sown, what is the probability that at least one fails to germinate?
questions.e: P(all 5 germinate) = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768, so P(at least one fails) = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.67232. 0.2 is the chance for a single seed only.

questions.s: A binomial distribution has mean 6 and variance 4.2. What is the number of trials n?
questions.e: q = variance ÷ mean = 4.2 ÷ 6 = 0.7, so p = 0.3 and n = 6 ÷ 0.3 = 20. 14 is nq, the mean number of failures, not n.

questions.s: Which of the following is not a condition of a binomial experiment?
o: p changes from trial to trial
questions.e: A binomial experiment needs a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same probability p of success. If p changes, as in drawing without replacement, the binomial model does not apply.

questions.s: A binomial distribution is symmetrical when:
questions.e: When p = q = 0.5, P(X = r) = P(X = n − r), so the distribution is symmetrical for any n. For p below 0.5 it is positively skewed.

questions.s: A Poisson distribution has mean 9. What is its standard deviation?
questions.e: For a Poisson distribution, variance = mean = 9, so S.D. = √9 = 3. 9 is the variance, not the S.D.

questions.s: X has a Poisson distribution with mean 2. Taking e⁻² = 0.135, what is P(X = 1)?
The number of calls to a helpline in a minute follows a Poisson distribution with mean 3. Taking e⁻³ = 0.05, what is the probability of exactly 2 calls in a minute?
questions.e: P(X = 2) = e⁻³ × 3² ÷ 2! = 0.05 × 9 ÷ 2 = 0.225. 0.45 forgets to divide by 2!, and 0.15 is P(X = 1).

questions.s: The Poisson distribution is most suitable for describing:
o: marks out of 100 in a test
outcomes of a single coin toss
questions.e: The Poisson model fits counts of rare events where there are many opportunities, such as misprints per page or accidents per day on a road. Heights are continuous and are better described by the normal distribution.

questions.s: In a batch of 200 items, each item is defective with probability 0.01. If the binomial is approximated by a Poisson distribution, what is the Poisson mean?
questions.e: The Poisson mean is λ = np = 200 × 0.01 = 2. 1.98 is npq, the binomial variance, which is close to but not the parameter λ.

questions.s: The total area under a normal curve is:
questions.e: The normal curve is a probability distribution, so the total area under it is 1 for every μ and σ. 0.5 is the area on one side of the mean.

questions.s: Heights of Grade 12 boys are normally distributed with mean 160 cm and standard deviation 5 cm. About what percentage are between 155 cm and 165 cm?
questions.e: 155 to 165 cm is μ ± 1σ, which holds about 68 % of a normal distribution. 95 % is the share within 2σ, which here would be 150 to 170 cm.

questions.s: In a test with mean 60 and standard deviation 10, Zainab scored 75. What is her z-score?
questions.e: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ = (75 − 60) ÷ 10 = 1.5, so she is 1.5 S.D. above the mean. 15 forgets to divide by σ.

questions.s: Heights are normally distributed with mean 160 cm and standard deviation 5 cm. Using the 68–95–99.7 rule, about what percentage are taller than 170 cm?
questions.e: 170 cm is μ + 2σ. About 95 % lie within 2σ, leaving 5 % in the two tails, so 2.5 % are above 170 cm. 5 % counts both tails.

questions.s: The points of inflection of a normal curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ lie at:
questions.e: The normal curve changes from bending downward to bending upward one standard deviation either side of the mean, at μ − σ and μ + σ. μ ± 3σ marks where almost all the area (99.7 %) ends.

questions.s: The standard normal variable Z has:
questions.e: Z = (X − μ)/σ shifts the mean to 0 and scales the standard deviation, and so the variance, to 1. A variance of 0 would mean no spread at all.

questions.s: Using the 68–95–99.7 rule, what is the approximate value of P(Z > 1) for the standard normal variable Z?
questions.e: P(−1 < Z < 1) ≈ 0.68, so the two tails hold 0.32 and each tail about 0.16. 0.34 is the area between 0 and 1, and 0.84 is P(Z < 1).

questions.s: The marks of 1,000 candidates are normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation 8. Using the 68–95–99.7 rule, about how many scored above 76?
questions.e: 76 = 60 + 2 × 8, so z = 2. About 2.5 % lie above z = 2, and 2.5 % of 1,000 = 25. 50 counts both tails, and 975 is the number below 76.

questions.s: The normal distribution is:
questions.e: The normal curve is a symmetrical bell with mean, median and mode at the centre. It has zero skewness, so it is neither positively nor negatively skewed.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.e: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. 0.9 forgets to subtract the overlap, which is counted twice.

questions.s: The table shows 100 students of a college by gender and group. A student chosen at random is in the Science group. What is the probability that the student is a girl?
questions.e: Given Science, the sample space shrinks to the 55 Science students, of whom 25 are girls: 25/55 = 5/11. 1/4 is 25/100, the chance of being a Science girl out of all students.

questions.s: A committee of 3 is to be chosen from 5 men and 4 women. In how many ways can it contain exactly 2 women?
questions.e: Choose 2 of the 4 women in ⁴C₂ = 6 ways and 1 of the 5 men in 5 ways: 6 × 5 = 30. 84 is ⁹C₃, every committee of 3 with no condition.

questions.s: A leap year is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has 53 Fridays?
questions.e: 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 extra days. The extra pair is one of 7 equally likely pairs (Mon–Tue, …, Sun–Mon), and 2 of them contain a Friday, so P = 2/7. 1/7 applies to an ordinary year, which has only one extra day.

questions.s: A fair die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
questions.e: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4, so P = 2/6 = 1/3. 1/2 counts 4 as well, but 4 is not greater than 4.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability of getting the same number on both?
questions.e: There are 6 doubles, (1,1) to (6,6), out of 36 outcomes, so P = 6/36 = 1/6. 1/36 is the chance of one particular double, such as (6,6).

questions.s: What is the value of ⁷C₃?
questions.e: ⁷C₃ = (7 × 6 × 5) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 210 ÷ 6 = 35. 210 is ⁷P₃, which forgets to divide by 3!.

questions.s: How many different arrangements can be made of all the letters of the word LAHORE?
questions.e: LAHORE has 6 different letters, so there are 6! = 720 arrangements. 360 halves the count as if a letter were repeated, but none is.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5. What is the probability that neither occurs?
questions.e: P(neither) = P(not A) × P(not B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. 0.3 is P(A and B), and 0.8 is P(A or B), the complement of the answer.

questions.s: X takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.25. What is E(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = 0 × 0.25 + 1 × 0.5 + 2 × 0.25 = 1. This distribution is symmetrical about 1, so its mean is the centre. 3 adds the values without the probabilities.

questions.s: A binomial distribution has n = 10 and p = 0.4. What is its variance?
questions.e: Variance = npq = 10 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 2.4. 4 is the mean np, and 1.55 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: A student guesses all 3 questions of a quiz, each with probability ⅓ of being right. What is the probability that exactly one answer is right?
questions.e: P(X = 1) = ³C₁ × (⅓) × (⅔)² = 3 × 4/27 = 4/9. 8/27 is P(X = 0), and 1/3 ignores the binomial calculation entirely.

questions.s: A Poisson distribution has variance 4. What is its mean?
questions.e: The mean and variance of a Poisson distribution are equal, so the mean is 4. 2 is the standard deviation √4.

questions.s: Using the 68–95–99.7 rule, about what percentage of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
questions.e: About 95 % lies between μ − 2σ and μ + 2σ. 68 % is the share within 1σ, and 47.5 % is the area on one side only.

questions.s: A box has 3 white and 5 black balls. Two balls are drawn together at random. What is the probability that one is white and one is black?
questions.e: Favourable pairs = 3 × 5 = 15, and all pairs = ⁸C₂ = 28, so P = 15/28. 15/64 uses 8 × 8, as if the balls were replaced; 13/28 is the chance of two balls of the same colour.

questions.s: A variable has mean 50 and standard deviation 4. What is the z-score of 42?
questions.e: z = (42 − 50) ÷ 4 = −2, so 42 lies 2 S.D. below the mean. The minus sign matters: 2 would place the value above the mean.

questions.s: A numerical value calculated from a sample, such as the sample mean, is called a:
questions.e: A statistic describes a sample and changes from sample to sample; a parameter describes the whole population and is fixed. The population mean μ is a parameter, while x̄ is a statistic.

questions.s: In simple random sampling:
o: every unit has an equal chance
only the largest units are chosen
units are chosen from one group
questions.e: Simple random sampling gives every unit of the population the same chance of selection, for example by drawing names by lottery. Picking 'typical' units by judgement brings in personal bias.

questions.s: A college divides its students into FSc, ICS and ICom groups and draws a random sample from each group. This method is:
questions.e: Dividing the population into similar groups (strata) and sampling randomly from every stratum is stratified sampling. In cluster sampling, whole groups are chosen and every unit in them is studied.

questions.s: From a list of 1,000 voters, a researcher picks a random starting name among the first 10 and then every 10th name after it. This is:
questions.e: Choosing at a fixed interval after a random start is systematic sampling. Stratified sampling would first split the voters into groups such as age bands.

questions.s: How many samples of size 2 can be drawn with replacement from a population of 4 units, if order is counted?
questions.e: With replacement, each of the 2 draws can be any of 4 units, so there are 4² = 16 samples. 6 is ⁴C₂, the count without replacement when order is ignored.

questions.s: How many different samples of size 2 can be drawn without replacement from a population of 5 units, ignoring order?
questions.e: ⁵C₂ = (5 × 4) ÷ 2 = 10. 25 = 5² counts samples with replacement, and 20 counts each pair twice.

questions.s: To halve the standard error of the mean, the sample size must be multiplied by:
questions.e: SE = σ/√n, so halving SE needs √n to double, which means n must be four times as large. Doubling n only divides SE by √2.

questions.s: Which result states that, for large samples, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal whatever the shape of the population?
questions.e: The central limit theorem says x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and SE σ/√n when n is large, usually 30 or more. The empirical rule only gives areas for a curve already known to be normal.

questions.s: The sample mean x̄ is used as a point estimate of the:
questions.e: A point estimate is a single value from the sample used to estimate a parameter, and x̄ estimates μ. The sample variance is itself a statistic, not something x̄ estimates.

questions.s: A random sample of 100 bags has a mean weight of 50 kg. The population standard deviation is 10 kg. What is the 95 % confidence interval for the mean weight?
questions.e: SE = 10 ÷ √100 = 1, so the interval is 50 ± 1.96 × 1 = 48.04 to 51.96 kg. 30.4 to 69.6 kg uses σ instead of the standard error, and 48.36 to 51.64 kg uses 1.645, the 90 % value.

questions.s: For a 95 % confidence interval for a mean with known σ, the value of z used is:
questions.e: 95 % of the standard normal area lies between −1.96 and +1.96. 1.645 gives a 90 % interval and 2.58 gives a 99 % interval.

questions.s: Other things being equal, a confidence interval for a mean becomes wider when:
questions.e: A higher confidence level needs a larger z (2.58 for 99 % against 1.96 for 95 %), which widens the interval. A larger sample or smaller σ narrows it, and x̄ only moves its centre.

questions.s: In a survey of 100 voters, half favour a new road. What is the standard error of the sample proportion, √(p̂q̂/n)?
questions.e: SE = √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100) = √0.0025 = 0.05. 0.0025 forgets the square root, and 0.25 is p̂q̂ before dividing by n.

questions.s: In hypothesis testing, the statement of 'no difference' or 'no effect' that is tested is called the:
questions.e: The null hypothesis H₀ claims no change or no difference, for example μ = 50. The alternative H₁ is what we accept if the evidence goes against H₀.

questions.s: A Type I error is made when we:
o: reject H₀ when it is true
accept H₀ when it is false
reject H₀ when it is false
accept H₀ when it is true
questions.e: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis. Accepting a false H₀ is a Type II error, and the other two are correct decisions.

questions.s: The level of significance α of a test is the:
o: probability of a Type II error
probability of a Type I error
questions.e: α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true), the risk of a Type I error we are willing to accept, often 5 %. The probability of a Type II error is β, and the power is 1 − β.

questions.s: A test of H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ > 50 is:
questions.e: H₁ points in one direction, greater than 50, so the whole rejection region is in the right tail. A two-tailed test would use H₁: μ ≠ 50.

questions.s: To test H₀: μ = 50, a sample of 64 gives x̄ = 52. The population standard deviation is 8. What is the value of the test statistic z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n)?
questions.e: σ/√n = 8 ÷ 8 = 1, so z = (52 − 50) ÷ 1 = 2. 0.25 divides by σ = 8 instead of the standard error, and 16 divides by σ/n.

questions.s: In a two-tailed z-test at the 5 % level of significance, the calculated value is z = 2.4. What is the correct decision?
questions.e: The critical values are ±1.96, and 2.4 lies beyond 1.96, in the rejection region, so H₀ is rejected. Moving to a 10 % level would not change this, since its critical value of 1.645 is even smaller.

questions.s: What is the critical value of z for a right-tailed test at the 5 % level of significance?
questions.e: In a one-tailed test the whole 5 % is in one tail, which starts at z = 1.645. 1.96 puts 2.5 % in each tail, so it is the two-tailed 5 % value.

questions.s: In the regression line y = a + bx, the coefficient b gives:
o: the value of y when x is 0
the correlation between x and y
the change in y per unit change in x
the mean of the y values
questions.e: b is the slope: y changes by b units for each unit increase in x. The value of y at x = 0 is the intercept a.

questions.s: The regression line of y on x is y = 5 + 2x. What is the estimated value of y when x = 4?
questions.e: y = 5 + 2 × 4 = 13. 28 adds 5 and 2 before multiplying by 4, and 11 uses 2 + 4 + 5.

questions.s: For a set of paired data, x̄ = 10 and ȳ = 25, and the regression line of y on x has slope b = 2. What is the intercept a?
questions.e: The regression line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), so a = ȳ − b·x̄ = 25 − 20 = 5. 45 adds b·x̄ instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: For 5 pairs of values, Σx = 15, Σy = 40, Σxy = 140 and Σx² = 55. What is the regression coefficient b of y on x?
questions.e: b = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) ÷ (nΣx² − (Σx)²) = (700 − 600) ÷ (275 − 225) = 100 ÷ 50 = 2. 2.67 is Σy ÷ Σx, which ignores the cross-products.

questions.s: The regression coefficients are b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45. What is the correlation coefficient r?
questions.e: r² = b_yx × b_xy = 0.36, and r takes the common sign of the coefficients, so r = +0.6. 0.36 stops at r², the coefficient of determination.

questions.s: The regression coefficient of y on x is −0.4. The correlation coefficient between x and y must be:
questions.e: r, b_yx and b_xy always have the same sign, because each has the covariance of x and y on top. A negative slope therefore means negative correlation.

questions.s: The correlation coefficient r always lies:
questions.e: −1 ≤ r ≤ +1, with ±1 for perfect linear relation. It can be negative, so 'between 0 and 1' is wrong.

questions.s: If the correlation coefficient between x and y is 0, then:
o: x and y are always equal
the points lie on a straight line
questions.e: r = 0 means no linear association. A curved relation can still exist, such as points following a U shape. Points on a straight line give r = ±1.

questions.s: For paired data, Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 18, Σ(x − x̄)² = 16 and Σ(y − ȳ)² = 36. What is the correlation coefficient r?
questions.e: r = 18 ÷ √(16 × 36) = 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75. 1.125 is 18 ÷ 16, which is the regression slope b_yx, not r.

questions.s: The correlation between x and y is 0.7. What is the correlation between u = 2x + 3 and v = 5y − 1?
questions.e: r does not change when a constant is added or when x and y are multiplied by positive numbers, so r(u, v) = 0.7. Only a negative multiplier would change its sign. 7 = 0.7 × 2 × 5, which treats r like a covariance.

questions.s: In Karachi, sales of cold drinks and the number of heatstroke cases rise and fall together through the year. This strong positive correlation shows that:
o: both may be driven by hot weather
questions.e: Correlation alone never proves cause and effect. A third factor, high temperature, raises both drink sales and heatstroke cases.

questions.s: In a scatter diagram, points that rise from the bottom left to the top right show:
questions.e: When y tends to increase as x increases, the points rise from left to right and the correlation is positive. Falling points would show negative correlation.

questions.s: Two judges rank 5 singers. The sum of squared differences of ranks is Σd² = 10. What is Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)]?
questions.e: ρ = 1 − (6 × 10) ÷ (5 × 24) = 1 − 60/120 = 0.5. 0.92 forgets the factor 6, and 0.52 uses n³ = 125 in place of n(n² − 1) = 120.

questions.s: The regression line of y on x is used to:
o: estimate x for a given y
estimate y for a given x
questions.e: The line of y on x minimises errors in y, so it predicts y from known x. To estimate x from y, the separate line of x on y is needed.

questions.s: The steady increase in Pakistan's population over several decades is an example of which component of a time series?
questions.e: A long-term, smooth upward or downward movement is the secular trend. Seasonal variation repeats within each year.

questions.s: Every year, sales of sweets in Lahore rise sharply in the weeks before Eid. This is an example of:
questions.e: A pattern that comes back at about the same time every year, linked to festivals or weather, is seasonal variation. Cyclical movements take several years to complete.

questions.s: Periods of business boom followed by recession, each lasting several years, form which component of a time series?
questions.e: Ups and downs with a period of more than a year, such as trade cycles, are cyclical. Seasonal patterns repeat within a single year.

questions.s: A sudden fall in crop output caused by an unexpected flood is an example of:
questions.e: Unpredictable effects of events such as floods, strikes or earthquakes are irregular (random) variations. They follow no regular pattern.

questions.s: A shop's yearly sales, in lakh rupees, are 10, 14, 12, 16 and 20. What is the second 3-year moving average?
questions.e: The second 3-year moving average uses years 2 to 4: (14 + 12 + 16) ÷ 3 = 42 ÷ 3 = 14. 12 is the first moving average (36 ÷ 3), and 42 is the moving total.

questions.s: A least squares trend line is y = 50 + 4t, where t = 0 in 2020 and t is in years. What is the trend value for 2025?
questions.e: For 2025, t = 5, so y = 50 + 4 × 5 = 70. 54 uses t = 1, as if 2025 were the next year after 2020.

questions.s: Using semi-averages, a series for 2015–2022 is split into 2015–2018, with average 20, and 2019–2022, with average 28. By how much does the trend rise each year?
questions.e: Each semi-average is centred at the middle of its half, at 2016.5 and 2020.5, which are 4 years apart. The yearly rise is (28 − 20) ÷ 4 = 2. 8 is the total rise between the two centres.

questions.s: Which of the following is a non-random (non-probability) sampling method?
questions.e: In convenience sampling the researcher takes whoever is easy to reach, so units do not have known chances of selection. The other three are all probability methods.

questions.s: Increasing the size of a random sample reduces the:
questions.e: SE = σ/√n falls as n grows, so the sample mean becomes more precise. The population's own mean and S.D. are fixed, and α is chosen by the researcher.

questions.s: All samples of size 2 are drawn with replacement from the population 2, 4, 6. What is the variance of the sampling distribution of the mean?
questions.e: The population variance is σ² = (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 8/3, and with replacement Var(x̄) = σ²/n = (8/3) ÷ 2 = 4/3. 8/3 is the population variance itself, and 4 is the mean of the sample means.

questions.s: The principle of least squares chooses the regression line for which:
o: the sum of squared vertical errors is least
the sum of the errors is greatest
the line passes through the origin
as many points as possible lie on it
questions.e: The least squares line minimises Σ(y − ŷ)², the sum of squared vertical deviations of the points from the line. The errors themselves always sum to zero, so that cannot be the rule, and the line need not pass through the origin.

questions.s: The standard deviation σ of a whole population is a:
questions.e: Any value describing the whole population is a parameter and is fixed. The sample S.D. s is a statistic, which varies from sample to sample.

questions.s: How many different samples of size 2 can be drawn without replacement from a population of 6 units, ignoring order?
questions.e: ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5) ÷ 2 = 15. 36 = 6² counts samples drawn with replacement in order.

questions.s: A population has standard deviation 15. What is the standard error of the mean for samples of 25?
questions.e: SE = σ ÷ √n = 15 ÷ 5 = 3. 0.6 divides by n = 25 instead of √n.

questions.s: A sample of 36 packets of tea has a mean weight of 80 g. The population standard deviation is 6 g. What is the 95 % confidence interval for the mean weight?
questions.e: SE = 6 ÷ √36 = 1, so the interval is 80 ± 1.96 = 78.04 to 81.96 g. 68.24 to 91.76 g uses σ in place of the standard error, and 78.36 to 81.64 g uses the 90 % value 1.645.

questions.s: A test is carried out at the 1 % level of significance. What is the probability of making a Type I error?
questions.e: The level of significance α is the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true, so here it is 0.01. 0.99 is the probability of correctly accepting a true H₀.

questions.s: The regression line of y on x is y = 20 − 3x. What is the estimated value of y when x = 5?
questions.e: y = 20 − 3 × 5 = 20 − 15 = 5. 35 adds 15 instead of subtracting it, and 85 multiplies 17 by 5.

questions.s: For paired data x̄ = 4 and ȳ = 18, and the regression line of y on x has slope 3. What is the estimated y when x = 6?
questions.e: a = ȳ − b·x̄ = 18 − 12 = 6, so y = 6 + 3 × 6 = 24. 30 is 18 + 3 × 4, the slope times x̄ added to ȳ instead of the change in x.

questions.s: The two regression coefficients are b_yx = 1.6 and b_xy = 0.4. What is the correlation coefficient?
questions.e: r = √(1.6 × 0.4) = √0.64 = 0.8, positive because both coefficients are positive. 0.64 is r², and 1.0 is the mean of the two coefficients.

questions.s: A correlation coefficient of r = 0.9 indicates:
questions.e: Values of r close to +1 show a strong positive linear relationship. r measures how closely points follow a straight line, not the ratio of y to x.

questions.s: For 4 students ranked in two subjects, Σd² = 4. What is Spearman's rank correlation, 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)]?
questions.e: ρ = 1 − (6 × 4) ÷ (4 × 15) = 1 − 24/60 = 0.6. 0.4 is the fraction 24/60 itself, which must be subtracted from 1.

questions.s: A population of 500 students is to give a systematic sample of 25. What is the sampling interval?
questions.e: Sampling interval k = N ÷ n = 500 ÷ 25 = 20, so every 20th student is chosen after a random start between 1 and 20. 475 subtracts instead of dividing.

questions.s: In stratified sampling, the population should be divided into strata whose units are:
o: equal in number in all strata
questions.e: Strata should be internally homogeneous, such as students grouped by class, so that a small random sample from each stratum represents it well. The strata themselves may differ from one another and need not be equal in size.

questions.s: Sampling error is the difference between:
o: a sample statistic and its parameter
questions.e: Sampling error arises because a sample is only part of the population, so a statistic such as x̄ usually differs from the parameter μ. It is not a mistake in recording; it shrinks as the sample grows.

questions.s: A population has standard deviation 12. What is the standard error of the mean for random samples of size 36?
questions.e: Standard error = σ ÷ √n = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. 0.33 divides by n = 36 instead of √n.

questions.s: For random samples from a population with mean μ, the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄ is:
questions.e: E(x̄) = μ, so the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean. σ/√n is the standard error, which measures the spread of x̄ around μ, not its centre.

questions.s: A Type II error is made when we:
o: reject H₀ when it is true
accept H₀ when it is false
accept H₀ when it is true
reject H₀ when it is false
questions.e: A Type II error fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false. Rejecting a true H₀ is the Type I error, whose probability is the level of significance α.

questions.s: If r = −1 for a set of paired data, the points of the scatter diagram:
o: lie on a rising straight line
lie on a falling straight line
questions.e: r = −1 is perfect negative linear correlation: every point lies on a straight line that falls from left to right. A rising line gives r = +1.
